text: Lie algebra cohomology is a cohomology theory for Lie algebras that was first introduced in 1929 by Élie Cartan to study the topology of Lie groups and homogeneous spaces by connecting cohomological methods of Georges de Rham to properties of the Lie algebra. It was later extended by Claude Chevalley and Samuel Eilenberg in 1948 to include coefficients in an arbitrary Lie module. If G is a compact simply connected Lie group, it is determined by its Lie algebra, and its cohomology can be computed from the Lie algebra via the de Rham cohomology of the complex of differential forms on G. This complex can be replaced by the complex of left-invariant differential forms using an averaging process, which are determined by their values at the identity and thus correspond to the exterior algebra of the Lie algebra with a suitable differential. This differential construction applies to any Lie algebra and defines Lie algebra cohomology for all Lie algebras, with a similar approach used for cohomology with coefficients in a module. For a simply connected noncompact Lie group G, the Lie algebra cohomology of its associated Lie algebra g does not generally reproduce the de Rham cohomology of G because the averaging process used to pass from all differential forms to left-invariant forms is only valid for compact groups. Let g be a Lie algebra over a commutative ring R with universal enveloping algebra Ug, and let M be a representation of g (equivalently, a Ug-module). Considering R as a trivial representation of g, the cohomology groups are defined via the Ext functor as the right derived functors of the left exact invariant submodule functor. Analogously, Lie algebra homology is defined via the Tor functor as the left derived functors of the right exact coinvariants functor. Important results include Whitehead's lemmas, Weyl's theorem, and the Levi decomposition theorem. If g is a Lie algebra over a field k with a left action on the g-module M, elements of the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex are called cochains from g to M. A homogeneous n-cochain is an alternating k-multilinear function f: Λⁿg → M. When g is finitely generated as a vector space, the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex is canonically isomorphic to the tensor product M ⊗ Λⁿg*, where g* denotes the dual vector space of g. The Lie bracket [⋅,⋅]: Λ²g → g induces a dual map dᵍ⁽¹⁾: g* → Λ²g* by duality, which defines a derivation dᵍ of the cochain complex by extending dᵍ⁽¹⁾ via the graded Leibniz rule; the Jacobi identity ensures that dᵍ² = 0, making it a differential. In this setting, k is viewed as a trivial g-module, and k ∼ Λ⁰g* ⊆ Ker(dᵍ) corresponds to constants. In general, let γ ∈ Hom(g, End M) denote the left action of g on M, regarded as a map dγ⁽⁰⁾: M → M ⊗ g*, and the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential d is the unique derivation extending dγ⁽⁰⁾ and dᵍ⁽¹⁾ via the graded Leibniz rule, with d² = 0 following from the Lie algebra homomorphism to End M and the Jacobi identity. Explicitly, the differential of an n-cochain f is the (n+1)-cochain df given by a formula where the caret signifies omitting that argument. When G is a real Lie group with Lie algebra g, the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex is canonically identified with the space of left-invariant forms with values in M, denoted Ωⁿ(G, M)ᴳ. The Chevalley–Eilenberg differential is then the restriction of the covariant derivative on the trivial fiber bundle G × M → G, equipped with an equivariant connection γ~ ∈ Ω¹(G, End M) associated with the left action γ ∈ Hom(g, End M) of g on M. In the case where M = k = ℝ with the trivial action of g, the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential coincides with the restriction of the de Rham differential on Ωⁿ(G) to the subspace of left-invariant differential forms. The zeroth cohomology group is the invariants of the Lie algebra acting on the module. The first cohomology group is the space of derivations modulo inner derivations, where a derivation is a map d from g to M satisfying a certain condition and is inner if it is given by d(a) = [x, a] for some a in M. The second cohomology group is the space of equivalence classes of Lie algebra extensions of g by M. Similarly, any element of the cohomology group Hⁿ⁺¹(g; M) gives an equivalence class of ways to extend g to a "Lie n-algebra" with g in grade zero and M in grade n. A Lie n-algebra is a homotopy Lie algebra with nonzero terms only in degrees 0 through n. When M = ℝ, the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex coincides with the de Rham complex for a corresponding compact Lie group, with M carrying the trivial action of g so that x a = 0 for every x ∈ g, a ∈ M. Finite dimensional, simple Lie algebras only have trivial central extensions. When M = g, the action is the adjoint action, defined by x ⋅ y = [x, y] = ad(x)y.
